You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

In your continual harness, entries created without global_=True belong to this session and are lost with it.

ID arc_task_09c578be_recolor_partial_stripe_row_suffix 
TITLE ARC task-09c578be: extend partial stripe rows through their trailing suffix 
 For task-09c578be, identify rows where a stripe-color run starts at the left edge and ends before the right edge, followed only by background cells. Recolor the entire trailing background suffix according to the demonstrated continuation. In the validated simple solid-stripe case, replace every trailing background cell with color 1; this solved rows with runs ending at columns 6 and 12. Do not recolor only alternating cells: that guess was incorrect. Some demonstrations show a repeating pattern in the suffix; when present, extend or recolor according to that explicit pattern rather than assuming a solid fill. Leave complete stripe rows, all-background rows, and all other cells unchanged. Preserve dimensions and infer colors from the task evidence where possible.

Additional confirmed periodic-suffix variant (correct test, 12×24; zero-based coordinates): background 3, stripe/template color 8, replacement color 1. Two rows contained alternating 8,3 patterns whose terminal 3 suffixes were longer than the expected continuation. Extend the explicit period into the suffix, replacing only the suffix cells where the continuation predicts 8 with 1 and leaving predicted 3 positions unchanged: row 7 columns 20 and 22 became 1; row 8 columns 19, 21, and 23 became 1. Every other cell remained unchanged. This confirms that a repeated pattern in the preceding row segment determines which suffix cells are recolored; do not fill the entire tail solidly, and do not alternate without evidence of that period.

Further demonstration evidence and unresolved test caution (2026-09-29): This task has broader cases than a simple left-edge solid bar. More demonstrations confirmed color 1 only in the trailing portion of selected incomplete stripe rows, while other rows with background tails remained untouched; do not recolor every non-background row or every row with any trailing background. Examples: (a) 30×20, background 9, stripe 8: row 0 has 8×4 then 9 tail, so tail becomes 1; full row at 20 remains unchanged. (b) 20×11, background 8, marker 0: row 8 has seven 0s then four 8s, and those four suffix cells become 1; the full 0 row remains unchanged. (c) 9×19, background 3, stripe 8: only the final row's suffix cells after a long run, a gap, and a final isolated 8 change to 1; a similar row that reaches the right border is unchanged. (d) 15×14, background 6, stripe 2: a partial stripe starting at columns 4 and 6 has only its trailing suffix changed (rows 6 and 10 zero-based), while other bars with trailing background remain unchanged. (e) 21×17: selected suffixes can be patterned rather than solid; in one row only alternating suffix positions changed to 1, using a period visible in the input. (f) 14×26 and 29×26 cases confirm a single final background cell after an otherwise full stripe may become 1, while other full stripes stay unchanged.

A 24×25 test (background 3, stripe 2) was NOT solved despite eight attempts. Failed guesses included solidly recoloring tails in all occupied rows; only rows beginning at column 0; only rows beginning with runs of length ≥2; only the middle sparse rows (indices 2,9,21); guessed periodic fills on sparse rows 3 and 22; solid fills on rows 1 and 20; and a guessed period-6 suffix fill on rows 1 and 20. Do not reuse those as established rules. A manually transcribed no-op grid was rejected as invalid dimensions, so it does not establish whether an unchanged output is correct. The remaining useful observation is that the input has three separated 3-row pattern groups (rows 1–3, 8–10, 20–22); identify stripe-row eligibility and continuation from demos rather than simply filling each row's trailing background. No correct output was obtained for this case.


ID arc_task_09c578be_horizontal_right_rays_unresolved 
TITLE task-09c578be horizontal rightward 1-rays: demos and failed hypotheses 
 Task task-09c578be: horizontal rightward 1-ray ARC rule (UNSOLVED; preserve as caution, not a validated solver).

This instance reached 8 wrong attempts. Seven demos all showed a stable high-level effect: preserve foreground cells and background, and place color 1 in background cells to the RIGHT of some qualifying foreground structure in the same row, continuing to the right edge. Full-width foreground rows stay unchanged. The hard part is determining which structures qualify; do not assume all foreground cells/runs or simple row-wise bars qualify.

Demo patterns observed:
- Demo 1: bg4, foreground0. Rows with solid horizontal bars/runs (e.g. row with 0s c0-5, row c0-9, etc.) had 1s replace background after the bar to the right edge; full-width 0 row unchanged.
- Demo 2: bg4, fg6. A row with 6s c3-11 and bg suffix got suffix changed to1; a row with c2-9 got suffix changed; rows with multiple separated 6 groups and a singleton rightmost cell did NOT get extended; a line reaching right edge unchanged.
- Demo 3: bg5, fg2. Rows 1 and 2 got a 1 at final column after fg ends at c7; row2 had separated groups c3-4 and c6-7. Full-width fg row unchanged; pattern ending at right edge unchanged.
- Demo 4: bg6, fg8. Rows containing a 4+-cell horizontal 8 bar and bg suffix changed suffix to1; full-width 8 row unchanged.
- Demo 5: bg9, fg2. Long horizontal bars of 2 with background suffix extended; full-width foreground rows unchanged.
- Demo 6: bg6, fg2. Rows with a solid contiguous right-end component (row4 c8-10 and row8 c9-12) got background suffix changed to1. Alternating singleton-like rows were unchanged.
- Demo 7: bg4, fg0. Horizontal bars from c0 to an endpoint with a background suffix got that suffix changed to1; full rows unchanged.

On the test grid (23x17, bg7, fg3), there were two prominent shapes: top around rows5-8 and bottom around rows18-21, with horizontal bars at row6 c0-10 and row19 c0-2 plus many separated/diagonal 3s. Multiple plausible interpretations were tried and ALL were wrong: (a) extend row6 and row19 prefixes only; (b) flood-fill 4-connected components and extend at component's global right edge, both with and without singleton components; (c) per-component rowwise rightmost contiguous run length>=2; (d) 8-connected components with rays from all rightmost cells. Thus none of those exact algorithms is validated. Do not repeat them without new evidence. The valid demos establish only the 1-ray effect, not the right object-connectivity or selection criterion.

Operational lesson: use examples to infer how foreground structures qualify; reserve attempts for distinct rule hypotheses. Check output shape with code before submitting: exactly 23 rows x 17 columns here. In this run, several hand-transcribed grids accidentally had one background row of width16 and were rejected as invalid ARC grids; generate/validate arrays programmatically.

# Refine

Refinement analyzes the conversation trajectory and applies small, evidence-backed
updates to the continual harness (prompts, memories, skills, subagent specs).
The implementation lives in the host (the same one behind the user's `/refine`
command); this skill is the kernel-side interface to it. Call it directly from
the Python REPL:

```python
await refine.status()
await refine.run()
await refine.run("create a memory about always checking git status before committing")
await refine.run("promote the error-handling pattern to a global skill", global_=True)
```

## API

- `await refine.status()` — current refine state as a dict: `pending` (whether a
  requested refine is already queued for this turn) and `in_flight` (whether a
  refine is currently planning or applying).
- `await refine.run(instructions=None, global_=False)` — schedule refinement.
  Returns `{"scheduled": True}` immediately, or `{"scheduled": False, "reason": ...}`
  when refinement cannot start. Optional `instructions` focus the refinement on a
  specific observation. Set `global_=True` to target the global harness store
  (cross-session); omit for local (session-scoped) refinement.

## Rules

- Refinement never runs mid-cell. A scheduled refinement runs when the current
  turn ends; the harness applies changes and rebuilds the system prompt, then
  resumes you automatically. Continue working normally after calling it.
- One request per turn is enough; calling `run` again before the turn ends only
  updates the instructions.
- Use refinement after observing a repeated failure, a reusable tactic, a
  repeated delegation role, or a behavior policy worth persisting. Do not
  rewrite the whole harness when a focused memory, skill, prompt note, or
  subagent spec is enough.
